newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany plays catch-up in EMU handicap stakes.
newsitem.headline: Germany plays catch-up in EMU handicap stakes.

text.p: Germany, long the front-runner in Europe's integration drive, is finding itself in the highly unusual position of having to reassure EU partners that it will indeed have the economic strength to lead them into the planned single currency in 1999.

Its economy, battered by a jobless crisis, high state spending and inability to push through key fiscal reforms, is even being parodied by countries like Italy, previously regarded as the sick man of Europe.

In an ironic role reversal, it was Bonn's man at Monday's meeting of European Union finance ministers in Brussels who had to reassure partners of the solidity of his government's pledge to meet the budget deficit target of the European monetary union's guiding Maastricht treaty.
Finance state secretary Juergen Stark said his government's forecast of a deficit of 2.9 percent of gross domestic product took account of "all recognisable risks".

But with commentators still musing over January's surge in unemployment to the highest since the 1930s, and Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition flailing over key reforms, doubts are mounting over whether Bonn can meet the three percent deficit goal.
Views on the issue among independent analysts fall into two schools.

One argues that Finance Minister Theo Waigel will be able to summon the political will to clamp down on state spending to meet the deficit goal, even if joblessness overshoots official targets and growth this year turns out lower than expected.
Then, the launch of the euro currency would be able to go ahead on time in 1999 with Germany leading a group of countries with a sound track record of fiscal and monetary prudence.

That view is held mainly by German-based economists, who also tend to see EMU going ahead even if Bonn misses borrowing targets. More sceptical analysts in Britain and across the Atlantic in the United States tend to see a German deficit overshoot forcing a delay in the whole EMU project.

January's shock unemployment data, which showed a 500,000 rise to nearly 4.7 million, were enough to persuade Holger Fahrinkrug of UBS in Frankfurt to raise his deficit forecast to 3.4 percent from 3.0 percent previously.
But, he told Reuters on Tuesday, monetary union will still go ahead on time by making use of the room for interpretation left open in the text of the Maastricht treaty.
Asked whether Germany would hit the three percent goal, he said: "No -- but they will still fulfill the deficit target."

Gerhard Grebe, at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt, expects Germany to achieve the Maastricht target. If it misses, he said Bonn -- despite its reservations -- would not be able to stop the so-called "Club Med" southern states like Italy and Spain from joining.
"One must see that a delay would have a devastating effect on other countries," he told Reuters. Failure to get EMU off the ground would leave "the whole world laughing at Europe".
Firmly in the second camp is Robert Prior-Wandesforde at HSBC James Capel in London, who sees Germany's deficit at 3.4 percent of GDP this year leading to a postponement of EMU.
If such a scenario plays out "it's crystal clear that they (Germany) don't want Italy in and would postpone EMU," he said.

Seizing on a chink in Bonn's armour, Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi visited Germany for the second time in two weeks on Monday, arguing strongly that his government's austerity measures should be rewarded with membership of the euro club.
"There is a difference between Italy and Germany. We have economic problems and I have prepared a strategy to solve them," Prodi told Reuters Financial Television.
The German coalition on Tuesday dashed speculation that it would freeze on state spending -- at least for now.
Such a measure, analysts say, would only be enough to save a few billion marks. "That does not meet the real scale of the problem," Fahrinkrug said.
Coalition leaders did agree, however, to try to cut welfare costs and plough more cash into job-creating investment.
Kohl on Monday meets leaders of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to try and unblock an impasse over tax reforms and spending cuts which stuck in parliament.
But positions remained wide apart on Tuesday.
Government spokesman Peter Haussmann restated Waigel's goal of cutting taxes by 30 billion marks ($17.6 billion) over the next two years to boost investment and growth.
But Joachim Poss, SPD finance spokesman, said Waigel's tax plans for 1998 -- published in draft form on Tuesday -- would open a multi-billion mark gap in state finances next year.
Waigel on Tuesday presented a draft tax reform bill that would bring forward 14 billion marks in planned tax cuts to 1998.
The bill, presented to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet, is part of a comprehensive two-stage tax reform plan agreed by coalition leaders to cut a total of 30 billion marks in taxes by 1999.
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097 150 ($ = 1.703 German Marks)
